title: Strength Has a Timing Side: Building a Parkinson’s Plan Around the Person
subtitle: A useful program is more than a list of lifts. Symptoms, medication routines, confidence and support can all shape how strength work fits into a person’s day.
imageAlt: A woman with Parkinson’s and a friend review a simple strength-training plan at home, with a sturdy chair and light weights nearby.

body: Strength is personal—and can vary by the hour

A strength plan for someone with Parkinson’s is not simply a choice of exercises and weights. Stiffness, balance, movement, energy and concentration may change how a session feels, and what is manageable at one point in the day may not work as well at another. A plan that ignores those differences can become difficult to use, even if its exercises look sensible on paper.

That is why the useful question is not only “What should I lift?” but also “What conditions help me do this safely and consistently?” The person with Parkinson’s is the expert on their own experience. Their preferences and observations should guide decisions about goals, timing and support. A partner or friend can help make the plan easier to follow, but should not assume the role of coach or decision-maker unless that is wanted.

The American Physical Therapy Association’s clinical practice guideline recommends progressive resistance training for people with Parkinson’s. But the guideline also notes an important limit: much of the research involved people in earlier or middle stages who did not have cognitive impairment. Its recommendations may not transfer directly to people with advanced disease or significant cognitive impairment; that is a reason to individualize the plan, not to rule out strength work altogether [1].

Evidence about one particular approach should not be mistaken for evidence about all strength training. A 2024 review reports that multiple forms of exercise have shown benefits across motor and non-motor symptoms in early- and mid-stage Parkinson’s disease [3]. That broad summary does not establish which strength-training plan is right for an individual.

The practical takeaway is measured: strength training is part of Parkinson’s rehabilitation guidance, but the best starting point and progression depend on the person, their needs and the available evidence.
Start with an assessment, not a shopping list

A physical therapist experienced in Parkinson’s can help connect a person’s goals with their current abilities and circumstances. That assessment may consider movement, balance, strength, daily activities, the home setting and whether another person’s assistance would be useful. An international rehabilitation consensus supports individualized exercise prescriptions across Parkinson’s stages, with progressive resistance exercise and assistance when needed [2].

Before an appointment, it may help to write down a few concrete goals. Examples might be carrying groceries more comfortably, getting up from a chair with less effort, or feeling steadier while handling household tasks. These are conversation starters, not promises that a particular exercise will achieve a particular result. Also note what tends to make movement easier or harder, and any concerns about falls, pain, fatigue or following instructions.

Ask the therapist what the plan is intended to address, how to recognize when an exercise needs adjustment, and when to check back. If the person already works with a care team, ask how the therapist will coordinate with them.
Find a time that fits the person’s day

Medication schedules and symptoms are individual, so there is no universal “best hour” for a strength session. Rather than assuming a standard window, the person can discuss timing with their clinician and therapist and observe how their own day unfolds. The aim is a workable arrangement, not a test of discipline.

A short log can make that conversation more specific. For a few planned sessions, note the time, whether the session happened, how movement felt, and any practical issue that affected it—such as a disrupted routine, poor sleep or an unexpected appointment. Keep the record brief and focused on patterns, not scores. If the person notices a consistent relationship between session time and how manageable the work feels, they can bring those observations to the therapist and ask whether a change is appropriate.

Do not change medication timing to fit exercise without discussing it with the prescribing clinician. The training plan should be adapted around the person’s care, not treated as a reason to alter it independently.

Progressive resistance training means that the challenge can increase over time. It does not mean every session must be harder, or that progress has to be measured by heavier weights. A therapist may select the movements, equipment, amount of effort and way to advance them based on an individual assessment. Those details matter: a generic set-and-repetition prescription would overlook differences in balance, coordination, symptoms and experience.

Ask the therapist to explain what counts as an appropriate challenge for this person, what signs suggest they should pause or modify a movement, and what to do if a session feels different from usual. Write down the agreed instructions in plain language. If the plan uses equipment, confirm how it should be set up and where it can be used safely. A clear record also makes it easier to resume after a break without relying on memory alone.

The person doing the training should be able to say whether the plan feels useful and manageable. If a movement causes concern or the plan no longer fits, bring that information back to the therapist rather than pushing through or making major changes in isolation.
Support that helps without taking over

A support person can reduce friction: help arrange a session, keep the written plan where it can be found, or offer a ride to therapy. But first ask what kind of help is welcome. Some people want company; others prefer to train independently. A family member’s presence is not automatically necessary, and it should not turn the session into a performance review.

If the person wants help tracking sessions, agree on what to record and who will do it. Keep the person with Parkinson’s in charge of the information and its use. At a follow-up, their observations—not another person’s assumptions—should lead the conversation. The rehabilitation consensus describes care that can include assistance when needed, while keeping exercise individualized [2]. That distinction matters: support is there to make the person’s chosen plan more workable, not to take ownership of it.
Build the handoff before the first session

Use a short, practical conversation with the physical therapist to make the plan usable. The person with Parkinson’s can name one or two goals, describe when movement tends to feel more or less manageable, and say what kind of help they want. Together, clarify the exercises and setup, how the person can adjust or pause, and who to contact with questions. Ask how progress will be reviewed and when the plan might need revisiting.

Then make the next step small and specific: schedule the first session at a time the person chooses, put the written instructions somewhere they can access, and decide whether anyone else should be involved. Afterward, notice what worked and what got in the way. That feedback gives the therapist something real to adapt. A Parkinson’s strength plan is not a fixed test of willpower; it is a collaborative approach to building activity around the person who will actually do it.
